combined_title: Reverie: The Student-led Exhibition Committee Fall 2026 Exhibition
description:
A reverie is a state between waking and dreaming, a moment when the mind drifts beyond the immediate. It is a space where memory, imagination, desire, and reality can overlap, distort, and take on new forms. In these moments, the familiar can become strange, and the ordinary can become something unexpected.

Reverie brings together student works that explore the space between what is known and what is felt. Across painting, oil pastel, ceramic, digital art, animation, and mixed media, the artists move through imagined landscapes, intimate encounters, memories, figures, and fragments of the everyday. These works blur the boundaries between observation and imagination, allowing emotion and perception to reshape what we recognize.

Rather than depicting dreams literally, Reverie considers dreaming as a way of seeing. The works reflect moments of escape, introspection, fantasy, and transformation, where the subconscious can surface and reality becomes open to interpretation. 

Reverie was conceived and curated by members of the Student-led Exhibition Committee (SEC), and features work by eight SEC members at the Stamps School of Art & Design. The exhibition includes ten works across oil on canvas, oil pastel, ceramic, digital art, digital animation, and mixed media.

event_title: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”
combined_title: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”
description:
Changes over the course of the nineteenth century in how Americans voted, from voice vote to public ballot box to private voting booth, also saw changes in the material culture that surrounded voting. Ballots and ballot boxes, campaign pins and ribbons, blank lists and pre-printed party tickets, lanterns and banners–the creative forces of the American print industry filled the country’s cities and small towns with the ephemera of electioneering.

As you look at the items in this exhibit, think about what they tell us about how Americans in the past felt about voting, and about how voting felt. How did Election Days feel when they were full of parades and music and public drinking? What was it like to vote when everyone around you knew who you voted for? And, most of all, who counted as a voter, and who did the counting?

On view September 11-December 22, weekdays from 12-4 pm.

combined_title: Adam Lenhart, carillon
description:
Graduate student Adam Lenhart performs on the Charles Baird Carillon, an instrument of 53 bronze bells located inside the Burton Memorial Tower. The largest bell, which strikes the hour, weighs 12 tons, while the smallest bell, 4½ octaves above, weighs just 15 pounds.

Thirty-minute recitals are performed on the Charles Baird Carillon at noon every weekday that classes are in session, followed by visitor Q&A with the carillonist. The bell chamber may be accessed via a combination of elevator and stairs. Take the elevator to the highest floor possible (floor 8), and then climb two flights of stairs (39 steps) to the bell chamber (floor 10). Hearing protection earmuffs are provided for visitors. Be prepared to walk on ice and snow in the bell chamber during winter. Built in 1936, the Charles Baird Carillon is not ADA accessible. Visitors with mobility concerns are invited to visit the Lurie Carillon.

event_title: Cosmo Whyte: Under the Quiet, Beyond the Eye
combined_title: Cosmo Whyte: Under the Quiet, Beyond the Eye
description:
Curated by Srimoyee Mitra

Stamps Gallery kicks off the fall 2026 semester with an ambitious mid-career survey of interdisciplinary artist Cosmo Whyte. Born and raised in Jamaica, Whyte completed a BFA from Bennington College and earned an MFA from the University of Michigan. He is currently a faculty member at the School of the Arts and Architecture, UCLA.

This exhibition brings together two central concerns that animate Whyte’s artistic practice: the archive, both personal and public, as a site of disturbance; and migration as a lived experience of refuge, refusal, and reinvention. In Whyte’s work, the archive is never static or neutral. Rather, it is a contested space where official histories encounter memory, inheritance, and the fragments of stories carried across generations. His practice moves within this charged interstitial terrain, between what has been recorded and what has been remembered, between institutional knowledge and embodied experience. Whyte invites the viewer to consider the fluidity of geographic borders and layered cultural identities that have persisted despite societal unrest caused by racial and socio-economic hierarchies across generations. In an era of intensified border politics and renewed debates over national identity, Whyte’s work offers a timely meditation on memory, movement, and belonging.

Presented with support from the U-M Institute for Humanities, the U-M LSA Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies, and the U-M Library.

combined_title: DCMB Tools and Technology Seminar by Abhirath Anand (Computational Medicine & Bioinformatics): "hospitraceR: An R Package for WGS-Based Genomic Epidemiological Analysis of Healthcare-Associated Infections”
event_subtitle: "hospitraceR: An R Package for WGS-Based Genomic Epidemiological Analysis of Healthcare-Associated Infections”
description:
Join us for the DCMB Tools & Technology Seminar Series featuring a presentation by Abhirath Anand from the Department of Computational Medicine & Bioinformatics. Enjoy a complimentary pizza lunch while learning about innovative research and cutting-edge tools.

"hospitraceR: An R Package for WGS-Based Genomic Epidemiological Analysis of Healthcare-Associated Infections”

- Tool Link:  https://github.com/theabhirath/hospitraceR

Abstract

Genomic epidemiology, which combines whole-genome sequencing (WGS) with patient data is becoming increasingly common to detect the transmission of hospital-acquired infections, especially multi-drug resistant organisms. As high-throughput WGS becomes more affordable, software that facilitates the analysis of this genomic data along with patient metadata becomes crucial to generate timely insights. Prior studies have shown that there can be many different approaches to detect transmission clusters with genomic epidemiology data, and oftentimes these approaches will have tradeoffs more or less suitable for a certain dataset. We present hospitraceR, an R package designed to facilitate such analyses. hospitraceR includes functions for detecting transmission clusters with two different methods, the standard SNV threshold approach and a threshold-free approach. It also includes functions that can use patient movement information through the facility to suggest potential transmission explanations for the clusters. hospitraceR seeks to enable users to use multiple methods of transmission cluster detection and compare them easily using cluster comparison metrics. Metrics like the adjusted Rand Index (ARI) and adjusted mutual information (AMI) have been included for this purpose, as has fraction of converts with shared source (FSS), a custom metric designed specifically for comparing transmission clusters. A companion package, hospitraceRvisualize, also includes opinionated plotting functions for certain commonplace visualizations that aid in epidemiological interpretations. We apply hospitraceR to a dataset consisting of 4 long-term acute care hospitals (LTACHs) from Chicago sampled for different periods of time as part of an intervention study and evaluate the two different approaches for cluster detection. We find distinct patterns exhibited by the transmission clusters in different locations and also compare the different clusters obtained with different SNV thresholds and linkage criterion for hierarchical clustering. The hospitraceR package proves to be helpful in facilitating such comparisons and makes it easy to use WGS data to aid epidemiological investigation.

description:
This presentation explores the vital role of Deaf professionals and the importance of communication access in the workplace. It will examine the growing presence of Deaf individuals in professional fields, particularly as accessibility, legal protections, and educational opportunities have expanded over time. Participants will also consider challenges Deaf professionals may encounter, including communication barriers, workplace accessibility gaps, and common misconceptions about Deafness. 

In addition, the presentation will highlight how American Sign Language (ASL) has evolved as Deaf professionals have entered new and specialized fields. As careers in medicine, science, business, technology, and other areas have become more accessible, ASL has continued to grow—developing new vocabulary and concepts that reflect the contributions and expertise of Deaf professionals. Overall, this presentation emphasizes the importance of inclusive communication, equitable workplace practices, and the continued advancement of Deaf professionals across diverse career fields.

Learn more about GCC Denmark: Inequality & Social Change at this info session with Senior Study Abroad Advisor Callie Rouse and Program Instructor Rebecca Christensen! 

Program Description: Denmark is consistently ranked among the happiest countries in the world and is known for its universal healthcare system, tuition-free education from kindergarten through graduate school, and open prison system. In this course, we will use a sociological lens to compare and contrast the education, public health, and criminal legal systems in the United States and Denmark.

During our three weeks abroad, we will examine the causes and consequences of racism, socioeconomic disparities, and other social inequalities within the Copenhagen community. By immersing yourself in Danish culture, you will learn about the country's unique norms, values, and policies, and how they differ from American ways of living. Through visits to community organizations, conversations with guest speakers, and cultural excursions, you will gain firsthand insight into Danish society.

By engaging in ongoing reflection and active learning, you will develop a greater awareness of your social identities within a global context, deepen your understanding of your own worldview, and consider your role as an agent of social change. Together, we will explore both the possibilities and challenges of applying Danish models of social welfare to create a more just and equitable society in the United States.

Students must enroll in SOC 225 Project Community: Sociology in Action in Winter 2027 as well to be eligible for this program.

event_title: NCKS Colloquium Series | Koreatown, NYC: The Consumption of a Transnational Brand
combined_title: NCKS Colloquium Series | Koreatown, NYC: The Consumption of a Transnational Brand: Jinwon Kim, Smith College
description:
Please note: This lecture will be held in person and virtually on Zoom. If you would like to attend via Zoom, registration is required. Once you've registered, joining information will be sent to your email. Register for the Zoom webinar at: https://myumi.ch/8JNPb

Synopsis:
In the past decade, Korean entertainment has gained global recognition, with Korean movies and TV shows winning Oscars and Emmys, and K-Pop groups becoming wildly popular. In Manhattan, Koreatown has become a popular destination for both locals and tourists, drawing them in with its bars, restaurants, and day spas. Jinwon Kim argues that Manhattan’s Koreatown has become a new type of ethnic enclave, what she dubs a “transclave.” This commercialized ethnic space exists solely for consumption, leisure, and entertainment, and has been shaped by South Korea’s nation-branding strategy, new economic and cultural strategies, patterns in Korean migration, and shifts in tourism and urban policies in New York City. Kim posits that for many consumers in Koreatown, especially those who are not of Korean descent, the space has become a commercialized place where transnational culture meets the diverse racial and ethnic mosaic of New York City. Kim emphasizes how the space functions to “brand Korea” as a space to “consume ethnicity,” reflecting the landscape of South Korea’s consumer culture through the physical appearance of buildings and stores and the inclusion of franchise brands. In this talk, Kim explores the recent popularity of Korean food in New York City by focusing on both transnational and domestic factors, leading to the new trend of commercialization of ethnic food, emphasis on authenticity, and rise of the omnivore society, by delivering the voices of ordinary people. While Koreatown’s authenticity has been largely defined by commercialized ethnic cuisine by local entrepreneurs, the Korean government, and franchises, Kim argues that Koreatown’s authenticity has represented the collective imaginations and narratives of various consumer groups–Korean nationals, Korean Americans, and non-Koreans.

Speaker Bio:
Jinwon Kim is assistant professor of sociology at Smith College. An urban sociologist and Asian Americanist, her research and teaching focus on race and ethnicity, transnational sociology, immigration, consumption, and qualitative research methods. Prior to her appointment at Smith College, she was a tenure-track assistant professor at the New York City College of Technology/CUNY (2019–2024). Her peer-reviewed scholarship has appeared in journals such as *City & Community* and *The International Journal of Cultural Policy*, and she is the co-editor of the volume *Koreatowns: Exploring the Economics, Politics, and Identities of Korean Spatial Formations* (2020). Kim is currently working on two book-length projects that investigate transnational culture and urban transformation. The first, *New Trends, Old Conflicts: New Black-Korean Relations in an Era of Global Racism and Global Media*, draws on 280 international interviews to examine anti-Blackness and interracial dynamics within the Korean entertainment industry, situating these conflicts within East Asian geopolitics. Her second project, *The Asian Times Square: Gentrification, Displacement, and New Ethnic Placemaking in Flushing, NY*, examines how waterfront megaprojects, transnational investments, and gentrification drive the physical and symbolic displacement of working-class East Asian immigrant families and small businesses. It also explores how these processes reshape inter/intraethnic relations among four East Asian groups—Koreans, Korean Chinese, Chinese, and Taiwanese—in Flushing, New York City.

event_title: Fixed Effects in the Tails (with Raffaella Giacomini, Annalisa Loviglio, and Yulong Wang)
combined_title: Fixed Effects in the Tails (with Raffaella Giacomini, Annalisa Loviglio, and Yulong Wang): Silvia Sarpietro, University of Bologna
description: Many economic decisions target units at the extremes, such as the most effective teachers, the worst-performing schools, or the most productive firms. These decisions often rely on fixed-effect estimates, but in short panels extreme estimates may reflect unusually large estimation error rather than extreme latent effects. We develop a semiparametric framework for identification and inference on the tails of latent group effects in short panels, where estimation error need not vanish. We show that within-group differences remove the group effect and provide observable information about the tail of the estimation error in group averages. This yields a conservative one-sided test of whether latent effects have a heavier tail than estimation error. Under regular variation and this tail dominance condition, tail estimators based on noisy group averages are asymptotically equivalent to infeasible estimators based on the latent effects. We use this oracle-equivalence result to derive frequentist inference for the Pareto exponent, extreme quantiles, and tail conditional expectations, and to establish consistent rankings of a fixed number of extreme units. We apply the method to administrative data on Italian middle schools to quantify the gains from replacing schools in the lower tail with average-quality schools.

combined_title: ChE SEMINAR: Ryan Hayward, *University of Colorado*: *Design and characterization of single ion conducting elastomeric networks*
event_subtitle: *Design and characterization of single ion conducting elastomeric networks*
description:
A reception with light refreshments will be held in the B10 lobby before each seminar from 1-1:30 p.m.

*Abstract:*
Our group has recently studied heterojunctions between oppositely charged ‘ionoelastomers’, i.e., low glass-transition polyelectrolyte networks, for applications including inherently stretchable and transparent logic elements, low-voltage electroadhesives, and electromechanical transducers. We have studied several classes of networks containing different polymer backbone, pendent group, and crosslinker structure and sought to better understand how chemical and structural parameters of the networks influence their device performance. In one example, we have introduced high mobility silicone backbones that lower the glass transition temperature and therefore improve conductivity of the materials. Remarkably, heterojunctions at the interface of polyanionic and polycationic layers of such networks exhibit strongly temperature-dependent rectification, providing insight into the critical role of interfacial polymer dynamics in the operation of these devices. In another example, we have introduced a modular route to prepare polyanionic networks that relies on Sulfur (VI) fluoride exchange (SuFEx) ‘click’ chemistry, enabling a systematic study of how ionic conductivity depends on the length of short perfluorinated pendent groups. A non-monotonic dependence is identified due to the competing effects of ion association and aggregation. Finally, we have studied a variety of different crosslinking species as a route to tune conductivity, stiffness, and toughness of these materials.    

*Bio:*
Ryan Hayward is the Department Chair and Hudson Moore Endowed Professor in Chemical and Biological Engineering at the University of Colorado Boulder. He received degrees in Chemical Engineering from Princeton University (B.S.E, 1999) and the University of California, Santa Barbara (Ph.D., 2004), and was a post-doctoral fellow in Engineering and Applied Sciences at Harvard University from 2004-2005 prior to joining the faculty of Polymer Science and Engineering at UMass Amherst in 2006, where he remained until relocating to the University of Colorado in 2020. His group’s work is focused on responsive materials and self-assembly, including the development of new approaches to optically- and electrically addressable polymers. Ryan received the APS John H. Dillon Medal (2014), the Journal of Polymer Science Innovation Award (2013), the ACS Division of Colloid and Surface Chemistry Unilever Award (2011) and was elected a Fellow of the APS in 2018. He was an Associate Editor for ACS Macro Letters from 2013 – 2022 and served in the chair line of the Division of Polymer Physics of the APS from 2021-2025.

The University of Michigan’s Leadership in Technology: Distinguished Lecture Series welcomes Nikesh Arora, chairman and CEO of Palo Alto Networks, a Fortune 500 company and global leader in AI and cybersecurity serving enterprises and governments worldwide. Arora will join Ravi Pendse, vice president for information technology and chief information officer at U-M, for a candid, forward-looking conversation about cybersecurity leadership in the age of AI.

AI is reshaping both sides of cybersecurity. It is giving adversaries powerful new ways to move faster, operate at scale, and target increasingly complex systems. At the same time, AI is becoming essential to identifying threats, strengthening defenses, and helping security teams respond with greater speed and precision. As cyber conflict begins to move at machine speed, how can organizations keep pace?

Drawing on his leadership at Palo Alto Networks and previous senior roles at Google and SoftBank, Arora will share his perspective on the evolving threat landscape, emerging trends, and AI’s rapidly expanding role in cybersecurity. The conversation will explore where cyber risks are headed, how defenders can prepare, and why technology alone is never the complete answer.

Attend in person at Rackham Auditorium for this timely conversation about how innovation, strategy, and human judgment must work together to secure what comes next.

combined_title: Biomedical Engineering (BME 500) Seminar Series: "When Nanoparticles Talk to Proteins: Learning the Rules of Nanoscale Recognition," with Angela Violi, Ph.D.
event_subtitle: "When Nanoparticles Talk to Proteins: Learning the Rules of Nanoscale Recognition," with Angela Violi, Ph.D.
description:
When Nanoparticles Talk to Proteins: Learning the Rules of Nanoscale Recognition

Abstract:
Whether a nanoparticle becomes a therapeutic, a diagnostic, or a toxin is decided at the moment it contacts a biomolecule. Our group has spent years developing molecular-scale descriptions of how nanoparticles form, what chemical identities they acquire, and how those identities govern their behavior in various environments.  Yet predicting where and how a given contact occurs remains slow and largely empirical: experiments are costly, atomistic simulations are computationally prohibitive, and existing computational models are built around protein-specific features that do not transfer to engineered nanomaterials.

I will first show what this molecular-scale view makes possible by examining one system in detail. Bacterial biofilms resist both antibiotics and mechanical disruption, in part because their extracellular matrix is reinforced by amyloid fibers assembled from phenol-soluble modulin peptides. Combining simulation with experiment, we found that graphene quantum dots form supramolecular complexes with these peptides, docking near the peptide N-terminus, shifting the peptide's secondary structure away from the alpha-helix, and preventing fibrillation, thereby dispersing mature Staphylococcus aureus biofilms without killing the individual bacteria.

Identifying such interactions one simulation at a time, however, does not scale. I will then describe NeCLAS, a machine learning framework that predicts partner-specific nanoscale interactions across chemical domains. By combining a coarse-grained structural representation with features that encode the physicochemical neighborhood at multiple scales, NeCLAS predicts protein-nanoparticle contacts more accurately than existing methods, remains competitive with protein-specific models for protein-protein interactions, and extends to nanoparticle self-assembly. Together, these efforts point toward rational, predictive design of nanomaterials for biological targets, and our ongoing work pursues both directions: deeper mechanistic understanding of nanoparticle interactions with bacterial communities, and broader predictive models that make such interactions findable by design.
    
Bio:
Angela Violi is the Dennis Assanis Collegiate Professor and Arthur F. Thurnau Professor at the University of Michigan, where she serves as Associate Chair for Research in Mechanical Engineering. She holds appointments in Mechanical Engineering, Chemical Engineering, Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, Applied Physics, and the Biophysics Program. Her research sits at the intersection of nanoscience, molecular simulation, and biology, using computational methods (from quantum chemistry and molecular dynamics to machine learning) to understand how molecular-scale processes determine the formation, transformation, and function of nanomaterials, and what happens when those materials encounter living systems.

Violi received her M.Sc. and Ph.D. in Chemical Engineering from the University of Naples "Federico II" in Italy. Before joining the University of Michigan faculty in 2006, she held research appointments at the University of Utah and at a Department of Energy ASCI center for science-based simulation of accidental fires and explosions. Her early work made foundational contributions to computational nanoscience, including multiscale models of carbonaceous nanoparticle inception and growth, as well as studies of the health effects of combustion-generated particles. In 2019, she led a U-M BlueSky Initiative that brought together engineering, medicine, microbiology, chemistry, and computational science to pursue nanoparticle design for health applications, the direction that anchors her current work.

Her many honors include the U-M College of Engineering Research Excellence Award, selection as Michigan's nominee for the Michigan Distinguished Professor of the Year competition, the ASME George Westinghouse Silver Medal, the NSF CAREER Award, and election as a Fellow of the Combustion Institute.

description:
Abstract:
The U.S. nuclear industry is entering a new chapter, driven by rising energy demand, renewed public interest, and unprecedented federal support. This talk will explore the forces behind today’s nuclear momentum, including efforts to deploy advanced reactors, strengthen domestic nuclear capabilities, and sustain the performance of the existing reactor fleet. It will also highlight the growing role of modeling and simulation in this evolving landscape. As innovative reactor concepts move from idea to deployment, predictive tools are increasingly essential for understanding system behavior, guiding design and licensing, and evaluating technologies for which experimental data remain limited. Together, public investment, industry innovation, and advanced computational tools are helping shape nuclear energy’s next act.

Biography:
Dr. Emily Shemon is a nuclear engineer at the Department of Energy’s Argonne National Laboratory. She serves on the extended leadership team of the DOE’s Nuclear Energy Advanced Modeling and Simulation (NEAMS) Program where she manages development, validation, and deployment of multiphysics tools for nuclear reactor analysis. She currently leads technical teams that develop high fidelity meshing software as well as fast reactor technology modeling capabilities. She co-leads the National Reactor Innovation Center’s Virtual Test Bed efforts, which supports industry adoption of advanced modeling and simulation through the open sharing of models. Dr. Shemon also has a background in high-performance computing and is on staff at Argonne’s Leadership Computing Facility. She is a graduate of the University of Michigan’s Department of Nuclear Engineering & Radiological Sciences where she received a Ph.D. in 2011.

event_title: Multiplicity: from binary to planetary formation
combined_title: Multiplicity: from binary to planetary formation: Dr. Daniella C. Bardalez Gagliuffi
description:
Most stars in our galaxy form in systems, whose architecture and composition are fossil records of
their formation and evolution. Particularly for brown dwarfs and exoplanets, belonging to a system is
a key advantage for their characterization and the calibration of evolutionary and atmospheric
models. In this talk, I will provide a status update on the multiplicity statistics within the 20pc
census, and lay out multiple ongoing efforts to characterize benchmark systems and confirm
candidate ones with Gaia-Hipparcos accelerations, double-PSF fitting, and spectral binary fitting
prior to the upcoming Gaia DR4. These benchmark systems are also our best atmospheric
laboratories to disentangle confounding parameters and their effect on spectroscopy. Together, these
studies bridge separate populations that look alike in their fundamental and atmospheric properties
but differ in origin, leveraging that contrast to trace their stellar or planetary formation histories.

event_title: DE Seminar: The Guderley Problem: Existence of Self-Similar Shock Solutions
combined_title: DE Seminar: The Guderley Problem: Existence of Self-Similar Shock Solutions: Jiaqi Liu, Umich
description:
Dating back to Guderley’s pioneering work in 1942, the Guderley problem is a classical problem in compressible fluid dynamics describing the implosion and subsequent reflection of a strong spherical shock wave. An initially converging shock propagates toward the origin, strengthens as it collapses, and eventually develops a singularity. After the collapse, an outgoing shock emerges and propagates outward.

In this talk, I will present our rigorous construction of self-similar converging and diverging shock solutions for the adiabatic exponent $\gamma\in(1,3]$. These solutions are analytic away from the shock interfaces and the blow-up point. The proof relies on continuity arguments, nonlinear invariances, and barrier functions.

event_title: Imaging Beyond the Electrode to Bridge Molecular and Macroscopic Scales using 2D IR Microscopy
combined_title: Imaging Beyond the Electrode to Bridge Molecular and Macroscopic Scales using 2D IR Microscopy: Amber Krummel | Colorado State University
description: Electrochemical cells rely on redox reactions at electrode–electrolyte interfaces, where electrode composition strongly influences reaction pathways and stability. Copper is widely used as a current collector, yet its interfacial redox dynamics in ionic liquid electrolytes remain poorly understood on ultrafast timescales. Traditional electrochemical techniques provide macroscopic insight but lack the temporal resolution to capture these dynamics. Here, we combine two-dimensional infrared (2D IR) imaging with theory to bridge molecular-scale dynamics and macroscopic electrochemical measurements.Using time-dependent 2D IR imaging, we probe ultrafast vibrational dynamics and chemical equilibria in an ionic liquid containing dicyanamide (DCA⁻). Although copper(I) is typically unstable in solution, DCA⁻ stabilizes this oxidation state, enabling the formation of both copper(I) and copper(II) DCA complexes under applied potential. Cross-peak analysis reveals dynamic equilibrium and migration of these species near the oxidizing electrode, permitting direct observation of reaction pathways during device operation. These results provide molecular-level insight into copper redox chemistry in ionic liquid electrolytes and demonstrate the capability of 2D IR imaging for studying operating electrochemical systems. Finally, we present a promising approach based on a spectral generalized master equation framework that dramatically reduces image acquisition time.

combined_title: FYRST Workshops 2026 - 2027: FYRST Workshop
description:
If you are only seeing one workshop, please SIGN-IN and refresh the Sessions page! If still having issues, click this link. 
First-Year Relationship and Sexuality Talk (FYRST) is a required, in-person, and peer-facilitated workshop that came directly from feedback and listening sessions with current University of Michigan students. Our goal is to create an accessible, supportive space for student-driven conversations where all identities and experiences are welcomed and in which students can build skills and tools around identifying goals and values and then communicate effectively about those. Workshops will be offered at multiple locations and times throughout the fall semester, so please sign up for the workshop that works for you!! First-Year Relationship Sexuality Talk (FYRST) FAQ:
“How many workshops do I have to sign up for?”
You only need to sign up for 1 workshop. Attending 1 workshop will fulfill the requirement for the training. 
“I see that there is more than one session, does it matter which one I sign up for?”
It generally does not matter which workshop you sign up for. There will be a few that are designated for specific groups such as transfer students or for students looking for accommodations. If you do not fit these groups please try to save these workshops for those that do and you are free to choose among any of the other workshops. 
“Is this workshop required?”
This workshop is required for all transfer and first-year students at the University of Michigan.
“I’ve experienced harm around relationships or sexual experiences in the past and I am worried that attending this workshop may be harmful for me.” 
Our team is aware that students who are coming into the university that have experienced harm in the past. Our workshop is specifically designed to respect and validate the experiences of survivors and has been carefully constructed to avoid any specific descriptions of violence and focus instead on themes of empowerment, communication, and boundary setting. However, if you still have concerns about programming and would like to request alternative programming, please feel free to reach out at SAPAC-FYRST@umich.edu.
“What if I struggle to learn in a presentation setting? I’m an active learner.”
Our workshop is built to meet a variety of learning styles, including time for self-reflection, small group sharing, and resources to take with you to work through on your own time! This workshop is meant to be interactive and inclusive. 
“Can I request accommodations?”
We considered accessibility in creating this workshop and selecting the locations in which the workshops are help. However, we recognize many places at the University are inaccessible and we've set an * next to workshops that are on the first floor and lack stairs. These workshops also will have a presentation (other workshops we do not) and are a good fit for those who might need a large font. Please sign up for those if you feel that accommodations would assist you and reach out to SAPAC-FYRST@umich.edu if you are concerned or have questions. 
“I missed my workshop, what should I do ?”
Our team tracks attendance at each workshop by having participants swipe in with their MCard. If you are not able to attend the workshop you signed up for, our team will continue to send reminder emails until you have completed a workshop. In this case, please sign up for another workshop as soon as you can as the workshop is required and may fill up especially near the end of the semester. No need to contact SAPAC unless you are not able to reschedule. 
“I have had gender-based violence training before, can I get this requirement waived?”
As this workshop was designed with University of Michigan student feedback in mind, our workshop is unique to the UM community. Our curriculum focuses on individualized reflection and because of its interactive nature, each workshop will be unique to the people attending. Although we are excited you already have familiarity with the subject, this workshop is required for every first year and transfer student. 
“I’m a commuter/non-traditional student, do I still have to attend?"
Yes, this workshop is required for every first-year and transfer student - not only do we want every student to benefit from having this time to connect with peers, but we also want to make sure your peers benefit from what you bring to our community. If you have any concerns or questions about being able to participate, please contact SAPAC-FYRST@umich.edu.
“I still have questions! Who should I contact?"
Please contact us at SAPAC-FYRST@umich.edu.

She is co-editor of the cross-referenced journal of narrative possibility, *The Encyclopedia Project,* and co-editor, with Ernest Hardy, of *War Diaries*, an anthology on black gay men’s desire and survival, published in 2010 by AIDS Project Los Angeles, and a finalist for a 2010 LAMBDA literary award. Her essays have appeared in exhibition catalogs for visual artists Laylah Ali, Jaime Cortez, Wura-Natasha Ogunji, Suné Woods and Cauleen Smith, and is forthcoming in the anthology *Letters to the Future: Black Experimental Women Writers*, and in a catalogue of site-specific art from The New School. She has done numerous presentations of cinema essays, most recently at ALOUD's "School of Prince" event at the Los Angeles Public Library, and at "Speak Nearby," a symposium of text and performance inspired by Trinh T. Minh-ha. Tisa Bryant was a commissioned writer/researcher for Radio Imagination, Clockshop’s year-long Los Angeles celebration of science fiction writer Octavia Butler, in collaboration with the Huntington Library in Pasadena, which houses the Octavia E. Butler Papers. She is working on *The Curator*, a novel of Black female subjectivity and imagined cinema. *Residual*, a meditation on grief, longing, desire and archival research, is forthcoming from Nightboat Books.

combined_title: What is a Classic?: Gerald F. Else Lecture
description:
I revisit the perennial question, "What is a Classic?" to consider the emotions and contemporary investments attached to professional classical studies and its popular counterparts. The success of the recent cinematic adaptation of The Odyssey demonstrates the ability of Greek myth and literature to still hold cultural value. But why? What is it about the classical that still compels? In the lecture, I depart from ideas of intrinsic value or heritage to understand what might be at the foundation of our cultural infatuation. I grapple with value as economic and emotional to understand what the classics are, where else we might find them across society, and why it is important to relocate value outside of the academic field of professional classical studies.

This lecture will be presented by Patrice D. Rankine, Professor of Classics, Committee on Theater and Performance Studies, University of Chicago.

A reception with light appetizers will begin at 5:00 pm, before the lecture at 5:30 pm.

Come curious, leave with a new appreciation for fangs and venom, just in time for Halloween.

combined_title: Best of FAMU: Eight short films created at FAMU, Prague’s film school
event_subtitle: Eight short films created at FAMU, Prague’s film school
description:
The program of short films offers a representative cross-section of works created at Prague’s film school throughout its eighty-year history. The eight selected films vividly illustrate the diversity of student filmmaking, encompassing fiction, documentary, and animation, as well as both lesser-known works and internationally acclaimed titles (including a Student Academy Award winner). Together, they span a wide range of styles and genres, from pantomime slapstick and historical drama to mockumentary and animated fantasy. The selection includes early works by filmmakers such as Jan Němec and Jan Svěrák, who went on to become major figures in Czech cinema, alongside outstanding talents from younger generations, including Daria Kashcheeva, Bára Anna Stejskalová, and Marie-Magdalena Kochová. 

List of films: 
• Encounter 
• The Loaf of Bread 
• Oil Gobblers 
• Closed Due to the Family Mourning 
• Pripyat Piano 
• Daughter 
• Love Is Just a Death Away 
• 3 MWh 


Film Synopsis: 

• Encounter (Vladimír Svitáček, 1953, 5 min.) 
Vladimír Svitáček, later renowned as a co-creator of the multimedia theatre Laterna Magika and the world’s first interactive movie Kinoautomat, depicts a crowded Prague tram in this pantomime-inspired comic sketch, featuring outstanding performances by the young Miloš Kopecký and Jiří Sovák. The film also includes rare archival footage of the area surrounding Prague’s Main Railway Station. 
Director: Vladimír Svitáček  
Screenwriter: Vladimír Svitáček  
Director of Photography: Jerzy Kotowski 
Original Score: Jaroslav Ježek  
Cast: Miloš Kopecký, Jiří Sovák, Jana Werichová-Kvapilová, Káťa Kopecká etc. 

• The Loaf of Bread (Jan Němec, 1960, 11 min.) 
This early student film by Jan Němec, one of the leading figures of the Czech New Wave, can be regarded as a thematic precursor to his masterpiece Diamonds of the Night. In the final days of the Second World War, a train carrying concentration camp prisoners stands at a railway station. Three exhausted inmates contemplate how to reach a nearby freight car loaded with bread, hoping to regain enough strength before attempting their escape. 
Director: Jan Němec 
Screenwriter: Jan Němec, Eva Límanová 
Director of Photography: Jiří Šámal 
Cast: Ivan Renč, Jan Bartůšek, Oldřich Bláha 

• Oil Gobblers (Jan Svěrák, 1988, 20 min.) 
Jan Svěrák’s Oil Gobblers was made in 1988 as his graduation film at the Department of Documentary Film. This mockumentary follows a fictional scientific expedition in search of an unknown creature known as the “oil gobbler,” whose very existence defies all the principles of life in a healthy natural environment. The film turns a serious ecological issue completely on its head, presenting its story with such convincing realism that the hoax is almost flawless. In June 1989, the film received the Student Academy Award presented by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. 
Director, Screenwriter: Jan Svěrák 
Director of Photography: Ladislav Štěpán 
Original Score: Vendula Kašpárková 
Cast: Lubomír Beneš, Jiří Němec, Ivo Kašpar, Jan Rokyta, Emil Nedbal etc. 

• Closed Due to the Family Mourning (Saša Gedeon, 1991, 9 min.) 
This short film by screenwriter and director Saša Gedeon is based on Alberto Moravia’s short story Fire. A bittersweet vignette, it portrays a single day in a small Italian barbershop on the eve of the Second World War. Rather than relying on an intricate plot, the film derives its power from its understated emotional tension and evocative atmosphere. Made during Gedeon’s second year at FAMU, the film received an award at the FFICS – International Festival of Film School Students in Tokyo in 1992. The prize money enabled the director to make his feature-film debut Indian Summer. 
Director, Screenwriter: Saša Gedeon 
Director of Photography: Miloš Kabyl 
Cast: Barbora Hrzánová, David Vávra, Jakub Špalek, Renata Beccerová 

• Pripyat Piano (Eliška Cílková, 2019, 18 min.) 
Many of the original inhabitants of Pripyat have never come to terms with the Chernobyl disaster. Some of them began composing their own songs and poems and returning to their apartments within the forbidden radioactive zone. This documentary concert, reflecting on the presence of a unique space, calls for the return of humankind as both creator and performer. In the poems and songs recited by the former residents of Pripyat themselves, a powerful connection between people and home can still be heard to endure. The film has been screened at major documentary film festivals and has received numerous awards. 
Director, Editor, Original Score, Sound Design: Eliška Cílková 
Director of Photography: Tomáš Frkal 

• Daughter (Daria Kashcheeva, 2019, 14 min.) This puppet animation by Daria Kashcheeva tells the story of a father and daughter who, despite mutual misunderstanding, eventually find their way back to each other. The film’s emotional intensity and unsettling atmosphere are enhanced by an unusually dynamic camera – rare in animation – and by close-up shots of the puppets’ faces, whose expressions feel remarkably lifelike. The film won the prestigious Student Academy Award (in the category of international animation) and was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Animated Short Film. 
Director, Screenwriter, Director of Photography: Daria Kashcheeva 
Original Score: Petr Vrba 
Editor: Alexander Kashcheev 

• Love Is Just a Death Away (Bára Anna Stejskalová, 2020, 10 min.) 
A dead dog, a landfill, and beautiful moths high in the sky – this is the world of Steve, a parasite desperately searching for a kindred soul. Yet every attempt at connection ends in disappointment. A small bird he saves from another dog dies. A rat that touches him dies. Cockroaches, under the guise of friendship, strip him down to the bone. Completely defenseless inside the skeleton of his former host, he nearly loses his life under the wheels of a machine that crushes waste. The film has screened at numerous festivals and received the award for Best Student Animated Short Film as well as the Audience Award for Best Animated Short Film at the Palm Springs International Film Festival. 
Director, Editor, Original Score, Sound Design: Bára Anna Stejskalová 
Director of Photography: Tomáš Frkal 

• 3 MWh (Marie-Magdalena Kochová, 2024, 13 min.) 
An employee at a nuclear power plant, obsessed with counting, sets himself a limit on how much electricity he wants to consume for the rest of his life. In this dark yet masterful cinematic poem shot on 35mm film, Marie-Magdalena Kochová presents the story of a man whose life is moving toward transformation. It is a tender acceptance of the idea that we are not only our bodies, but also energy. The film has been screened at numerous international festivals and Czech Film Critics Award. 
Director: Marie-Magdalena Kochová 
Screenwriter: Josef Kokta 
Director of Photography: Kristina Kůlová 
Original Score: Haštal Hapka 
Cast: Jaroslav Pížl

combined_title: Paris is Burning: Humanities Film Series
description:
Where does voguing come from, and what, exactly, is throwing shade? This landmark documentary provides a vibrant snapshot of the 1980s through the eyes of New York City’s African American and Latinx Harlem drag ball scene. Made over seven years, *Paris Is Burning *offers an intimate portrait of rival fashion “houses,” from fierce contests for trophies to house mothers offering sustenance in a world rampant with homophobia and transphobia, racism, AIDS, and poverty. Featuring legendary voguers, drag queens, and trans women—including Willi Ninja, Pepper LaBeija, Dorian Corey, and Venus Xtravaganza—*Paris Is Burning *brings it, celebrating the joy of movement, the force of eloquence, and the draw of community.

Digitally remastered by the UCLA Film and Television Archive in conjunction with Sundance Institute and Outfest UCLA Legacy Project. Preservation funded by Sundance Institute, Outfest, and the Andrew J. Kuehn Jr. Foundation.
